Most towns were built around the church, the center of community life.
en.colonyRegions2: Middle Colonies The land ranged from rich coastal soil to forests and valleys, perfect for farming and trade. People grew crops, raised animals, and worked in logging and shipbuilding. Settlers here came from many cultures and religions, making the region very diverse.
en.colonyRegions3: Southern Colonies Broad rivers, warm weather, and fertile soil made this region perfect for farming. Wealthy colonists built large farms called plantations. en.colonyRegionsSpeak:
Each region has its own way of life. Read the descriptions and find what makes them different!

Middle Colonies
New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware
Home to a mix of cultures and religions, the Middle Colonies had fertile soil, valleys, and wooded mountains. Farmers grew diverse crops and raised livestock, while industries such as logging and shipbuilding also thrived. Known as the “breadbasket colonies,” they were more diverse and tolerant than other regions.

New England Colonies
Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Hampshire
Founded largely by settlers seeking religious freedom, this region had long, cold winters and rocky, hilly land, making large-scale farming difficult. Its economy relied on small farms, logging, fishing, shipbuilding, and trade. Communities often centered around the church, which played a role in both religious and political life.

Southern Colonies
Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia
With a warm, wet climate and fertile soil, the Southern Colonies focused on agriculture, especially cash crops like tobacco, rice, and indigo. Large plantations dominated the economy, relying on the labor of enslaved Africans and indentured servants. Rivers made it easy to ship goods directly to coastal ports.
